title: Noncyclic geometric phase in three-level Ramsey interferometry for enhanced metrology
abstract: In a standard two-level Ramsey interferometer, the measured phase accumulates linearly during the interrogation time. Here, we introduce three-level Ramsey interferometry that employs a noncyclic geometric phase response to enhance phase sensing, with projected internal-path interference reshaping the mapping from accumulated signal phase to readout phase. Near a geodesic-closure transition, a small accumulated signal phase produces a sharply amplified readout-phase shift. We quantify the accompanying gain--visibility tradeoff and identify a finite operating window in which the amplified response yields a net signal-to-noise-ratio gain under technical-noise-limited conditions. By tuning an initial Ramsey phase offset, this high-slope window can be positioned at a desired operating point and sampled repeatedly with shorter cycles, providing a geometric shortcut to improved projected stability. More broadly, these results establish a multilevel Ramsey route to enhanced phase sensitivity in quantum platforms, where two signal-collecting internal paths interfere to produce a noncyclic geometric response.
summary: The paper introduces enhanced phase sensing in three-level Ramsey interferometers by utilizing a noncyclic geometric phase response. By analyzing the interference between two internal paths, researchers derive a mechanism that sharply amplifies the readout phase near specific operating points. This allows for a projected improvement in measurement stability compared to standard methods, provided external technical noise is present.
main_problem: The goal is to enhance phase sensing sensitivity beyond standard linear accumulation by exploiting a noncyclic geometric phase response in Ramsey interferometry.
main_result: A net Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) gain can be achieved only within a finite operating window where the enhanced local phase slope compensates for visibility reduction and technical noise. This allows for a 'geometric shortcut' to improved projected stability via faster sampling cycles.
method: The analysis models the three-level system interference, deriving effective fringe visibility ($V_s$) and readout phase ($\Phi$). Sensitivity is quantified by analyzing the local phase-response gain versus noise penalties.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a three-level Ramsey interferometer. The mechanism relies on the interference of amplitudes from two signal-collecting internal paths onto a shared readout channel, generating a noncyclic geometric phase jump near a geodesic-closure transition.
key_observables: Readout phase $\Phi(\phi)$, projected visibility $V_s(\phi)$, inferred signal-phase uncertainty ($\Delta\phi$), and the net SNR enhancement factor ($E$).
important_parameters: Pathway imbalance ($\epsilon = A_1 - A_2$), technical noise level ($\xi_{CLA}$), and the initial Ramsey phase offset ($\phi_{	ext{off}}$).
main_assumptions: The technique's utility is shown to be most pronounced when additive classical phase noise ($\xi_{CLA}$) is present, as this external noise source can be leveraged by the geometric enhancement.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the gain–visibility tradeoff (showing $G_{max}^N$ vs. $V_{min}$), map the finite SNR enhancement window, and compare projected fractional instability for standard versus shortcut protocols.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from deriving the effective fringe structure ($P_s(t)$) to quantifying the local phase-response gain ($G_N$). It then analyzes the trade-off between this gain and visibility loss. Finally, it applies these findings to predict a measurable improvement in clock stability using an offset-controlled 'shortcut protocol'.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, theoretically derived method for engineering quantum sensors by manipulating geometric phase accumulation, offering a pathway to surpass standard metrological limits in atomic systems.
